title: Viral Rat-in-Dosa Video Was an Extortion Plot, Mumbai Police Allege
excerpt: Days after a viral video allegedly showing a dead rat in a dosa cost Borivali's Radhakrishna Hotel its food licence, Mumbai police say the woman behind the complaint was caught red-handed accepting Rs 6 lakh in what they call an extortion bid.
body:
• On September 24, Mansi Acharya alleged she found a dead rat in a Mysore Masala Dosa at Radhakrishna Hotel in Mumbai's Borivali, after her brother had already eaten a few bites and vomited; a video of the incident went viral.
  • Taking cognisance of the footage, the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration suspended the eatery's licence on September 28, amid a wider festive-season hygiene crackdown led by FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe.
  • The hotel owner told police he then received repeated calls demanding Rs 25 lakh to suppress the video, threats that were also made to his relatives; after agreeing to a Rs 6 lakh settlement and paying Rs 1 lakh in cash, he filed a complaint on September 29.
  • Borivali Police laid a trap and caught Acharya, 36, red-handed while she was accepting the remaining Rs 6 lakh; police say she is the prime accused and are investigating the roles of other accused individuals.

Mumbai police have arrested the woman behind a viral video that allegedly showed a dead rat inside a dosa at a Borivali eatery, accusing her of trying to extort the hotel owner just days after the footage cost the establishment its food licence.

According to a report by NDTV cited by the Daily Jagran, Mansi Acharya, 36, visited Radhakrishna Hotel in Borivali on September 24 with two men and a child. Her family alleged that her brother had already eaten a few bites of a Mysore Masala Dosa when he spotted a small dead rat inside it and began vomiting. Acharya called the Borivali police station to report the matter, and a video of the incident soon spread across social media.

Context & Background

The video triggered swift regulatory action. Taking cognisance of the viral footage, the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration suspended the hotel's licence on September 28. The incident landed in the middle of a broader inspection drive by the FDA across the state during the festive season, led by FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe.

The case also drew political noise. Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut alleged corruption among enforcement officials, claiming bribes worth lakhs were being demanded to revoke closure notices or restore licences. Mundhe rejected the charges, asserting zero tolerance for corruption while demanding concrete evidence to act against erring officials, according to India Today.

Then came the twist. The hotel owner claimed that after the incident he began receiving calls demanding Rs 25 lakh in compensation, with threats to release the video and even calls to his relatives to spread news of the incident. Mentally harassed through repeated phone calls, he agreed to settle for Rs 6 lakh, paid Rs 1 lakh in cash, and then filed a police complaint on September 29.

Impact & Analysis

Borivali Police laid a trap. The woman was called to collect the remaining Rs 6 lakh, and officers caught her red-handed while accepting the cash. Investigators say the prime accused is the same woman who had ordered the food in the hotel, and legal proceedings have been initiated. Police are also examining the roles of other accused individuals.

"The hotel owner told police the viral video had pushed the business to the verge of closure."

— the hotel owner, in his statement to Borivali Police

The case leaves uncomfortable questions on both sides. If the contamination claim was genuine, a real food-safety violation occurred and the licence suspension stands on its own merits. If the complaint was staged or leveraged, it amounts to using a regulator's enforcement machinery as pressure for extortion. Either way, the episode shows how a single smartphone video can move a restaurant from serving customers to shuttered in four days — faster than any laboratory verification of what was actually in the food.

Diaspora Angle

For NRIs who dine out on trips home, the case is a reminder that Mumbai's food-safety enforcement can move fast on viral complaints — and that a licence suspension driven by social media footage is not the same as a verified finding. Checking for displayed FSSAI or FDA licences remains the simplest consumer check.

What's Next

The extortion probe is now in the police's hands, with Acharya in custody and the roles of the two men who accompanied her on September 24 under examination. The hotel's licence remains suspended, and the FDA's wider festive-season crackdown across Maharashtra continues.
